strengths: Novel formulation of symmetry discovery as conditional flow matching on Lie groups, learning a distribution over a hypothesis group G whose support corresponds to the true symmetry subgroup H.
Unified framework for continuous and discrete symmetries, including reflections via flow matching over the complex domain, which is a creative extension.

Identifies and empirically analyzes the 'last-minute mode convergence' phenomenon, using posterior entropy and velocity fields to explain why the learned vector field remains near zero for most timesteps.
Honest limitations section discussing failure cases (e.g., octahedral without schedule, icosahedral with schedule) and open challenges for scaling to noisy real-world data.
Demonstrates success on simple 2D/3D point-cloud datasets for C4, D4, Tet, and SO(2), and reports Wasserstein-1 distances outperforming the LieGAN baseline in several settings.
weaknesses: Technical inconsistency between the main text and Appendix A: the main text defines the path as x_t = exp(tA)x0 (left multiplication on data), while Appendix A derives the target field using the group curve g_t = g exp(tA) and left-invariant pushforward, which corresponds to a different data path (g exp(tA)x1). The derivation therefore does not match Algorithm 1, undermining the theoretical justification of the method.

Inconsistent sampling update: the text states x_{t+Δt} = x_t exp(Δt A_t) (right multiplication), whereas Algorithm 2 uses exp(Δt A_t) x_t (left multiplication). This ambiguity harms reproducibility and clarity.

Evidential inconsistency: Table 2 reports a low Wasserstein-1 distance for SO(3) -> Oct (0.0962), but Section 5.2 explicitly states the model fails to discover Oct with uniform time and only succeeds after introducing the power schedule. It is unclear whether Table 2 uses the schedule; if not, the result contradicts the text. No W1 is reported for the Ico failure case.

Limited evaluation: experiments are restricted to synthetic, noise-free point clouds; no real-world or noisy data. The only baseline is LieGAN, with no comparison to the closest related method (Allingham et al., 2024) or other symmetry discovery approaches. No statistical significance tests or error bars.

The proposed power time schedule is heuristic: no ablation on the skewness parameter n, no comparison to alternative schedules, and only n=5 is tested. It enables Oct discovery but still fails for the icosahedral group (60 elements), so scalability to higher-order symmetries remains unresolved.
Reproducibility is weak: no code release and no full hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, epochs, network widths, optimizer) are provided, making independent reproduction difficult.

Claims of being 'more flexible' and requiring 'fewer assumptions' are overstated: the method still assumes a known hypothesis group G that contains the true symmetry group H, and it cannot discover symmetries outside G. It also fails on higher-order subgroups.

The analysis of last-minute mode convergence is conducted only on a 1D toy problem (SO(2) -> C4). It is unclear how the phenomenon generalizes to higher-dimensional or non-commutative groups, limiting the generality of the central insight.

strengths: Novel formulation of symmetry discovery as conditional flow matching on Lie groups, learning a distribution over a hypothesis group G that concentrates on the data symmetry subgroup H. This unifies continuous and discrete symmetry discovery within one objective.

The method can handle reflections by performing flow matching over the complex domain (GL(2,C) -> D4), which is a technically interesting extension and successfully recovers all 8 D4 elements in the 2D experiments.

The analysis of 'last-minute mode convergence' is a useful insight: because target modes are symmetrically arranged, the marginal target velocity averages near zero for most of the flow, and the posterior remains nearly uniform until t approaches 1. The simplified SO(2)->C4 group-element experiment provides direct evidence for this phenomenon.

The proposed power time schedule is a simple and practical heuristic that enables discovery of the octahedral group in one setting, showing that the issue can be partially mitigated by sampling more timesteps near t=1.
The framework is group-agnostic in principle: the same flow-matching objective is applied to SO(2), GL(2,R)+, GL(2,C), and SO(3) prior groups with only architecture and prior changes.
The limitations section is honest about several important issues, including scaling to noisy real-world data, restriction to the hypothesis group, and unresolved failure on higher-order groups.
LLM usage is explicitly disclosed, which is good practice.
weaknesses: There is a major inconsistency between the narrative and the quantitative results. Section 5.2 and the Discussion state that the model fails for the octahedral group and learns a nearly uniform distribution over SO(3) (Figure 5b), yet Table 2 reports a Wasserstein-1 distance of 0.0962 for SO(3)->Oct, which is comparable to the successful Tet result (0.0885) and far better than LieGAN (1.682). It is not clarified whether Table 2 uses the power schedule for Oct; if it does, the table is not comparable to the stated failure case, and if it does not, the table contradicts the text. This undermines the paper's central empirical claims.

Reproducibility is very weak. There is no code release, no random seeds, no error bars, and no detailed hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, optimizer, training steps, network widths). Appendix B only describes the network as a 'small MLP' or 'wider network' and omits most training details. Single-run Wasserstein distances are reported without uncertainty.

The empirical evaluation is extremely narrow: only noise-free, simple 2D/3D point clouds of canonical objects. There are no experiments on noisy data, approximate symmetries, real-world scans, or higher-dimensional data, despite the abstract's motivation about partial or noisy real-world scans. The method's claimed advantage for approximate symmetries is not demonstrated.

The baseline comparison is insufficient. Only LieGAN is compared; there is no comparison to closely related methods such as Allingham et al. (2024), which the paper itself calls 'the closest to our method', nor to Ko et al. (2024), Shaw et al. (2024), or Benton et al. (2020). Details of how group elements are sampled from LieGAN are missing, making the comparison hard to assess.

The method cannot discover symmetries outside the predefined hypothesis group G; it only finds subgroups of G. The title 'Discovering Lie Groups' and the abstract overstate the contribution, since the Lie group itself is assumed known. The limitations section admits this, but the main claims are not adjusted accordingly.

The method fails on higher-order groups: octahedral without the heuristic, and icosahedral even with the power schedule. The power schedule uses n=5 with no sensitivity analysis or theoretical justification. This leaves the scalability of the approach to complex symmetries unresolved.

The theoretical derivation has problems. Equation 7's target vector field with a 1/(1-t) factor is not the derivative of the interpolation in Equation 6 for general g0,g1; it only coincidentally matches in their special case g1=e. The derivation is therefore sloppy and potentially misleading. In addition, the objective compares network outputs to A, but A is not identifiable from x_t alone; the method implicitly relies on a marginal expectation that is not clearly explained.

The paper's presentation has serious issues. The reference list is corrupted with repeated 'Gass and Gass' entries and numerous citation/year mismatches (e.g., Benton et al. 2025 vs 2020, Allen vs Allingham, Chen and Upman vs Chen and Lipman). There are typos such as 'comapre', and the power distribution is described incorrectly as 'p(x)=nx^{n-1}, x~U(0,1)', which is mathematically contradictory. Figures are small and difficult to interpret.

Algorithm 2 requires an initial data sample x1 to generate a new sample, so the method is not a standard generative model from a fixed prior; it is closer to a canonicalization/inversion procedure. The abstract's claim about 'generation of new plausible data' is therefore somewhat misleading.

The 'last-minute mode convergence' analysis is only performed for a 1D flow on group elements, not for the data-space flow used by the method. The posterior computation uses a Gaussian approximation at t≈1 with σ=0.1, which may influence the conclusions. The extension to data space is plausible but not directly verified.

The claim that the method 'requires fewer assumptions' is not well supported: it assumes a known hypothesis group, exact invariance, no noise, connected/compact groups for uniform priors, and access to the data distribution. These are substantial assumptions, especially compared to methods that learn generators or symmetries more flexibly.

strengths: Novel formulation of symmetry discovery as flow matching on Lie groups, learning a distribution over a larger hypothesis group G that concentrates on the true symmetry subgroup H, avoiding adversarial training and likelihood-based objectives.
Unified treatment of continuous and discrete symmetries, with successful demonstrations on 2D C4 and D4 (including reflections via a complex-domain flow) and 3D tetrahedral and SO(2) symmetries.

Identification and analysis of the 'last-minute mode convergence' phenomenon, where the target vector field remains near zero until t≈1 due to symmetric multi-modal targets, and proposal of a power time schedule that enables discovery of the octahedral group.
Honest discussion of limitations and failures (e.g., failure on the icosahedral group, octahedral group with uniform time sampling), which is valuable for future work.
The method is clearly described with training/generation algorithms and a derivation of the target vector field in Appendix A.
weaknesses: Empirical evaluation is limited to synthetic, noise-free, low-dimensional point clouds (2D/3D). No real-world datasets or higher-dimensional problems are considered, so practical significance and scalability remain unproven.

Quantitative results are inconsistent with qualitative claims. Table 2 reports a low Wasserstein-1 distance (0.0962) for SO(3)→Oct, yet the text states the model fails and learns a uniform distribution over SO(3). Table 1 shows LieFlow (1.321) is worse than LieGAN (1.131) for GL(2,R)+→C4, contradicting the claim that it outperforms LieGAN in all experiments.

The complex-domain method for reflections is not clearly explained. GL(2,C) as complex linear maps on 2D data cannot represent orientation-reversing reflections; the paper does not specify how the group acts on complexified data or how reflections are achieved, making the D4 result difficult to reproduce or assess.

Only one baseline (LieGAN) is compared, despite discussing several other symmetry discovery methods (e.g., Allingham et al. 2024, Benton et al., Ko et al.). The closest work (Allingham et al.) is not empirically compared.

Reproducibility is limited: no code release, no hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, optimizer, architecture details), no compute resources, and no random seeds. The LLM usage is disclosed, but the code is not available.

The power time schedule is heuristic (n=5) with no ablation or principled selection, and it still fails for the icosahedral group, so the core challenge of scaling to higher-order groups remains unresolved.

The theoretical analysis of 'last-minute mode convergence' is conducted on a simplified 1D flow matching on group elements, not on the proposed LieFlow method on data space. It is illustrative but not a rigorous analysis of the actual algorithm.

The method assumes a known, connected hypothesis group G that contains the true symmetry H. The paper does not study sensitivity to the choice of G or the prior distribution, which is a strong practical limitation.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated reformulation of symmetry discovery as distribution learning over a hypothesis Lie group, where the support of the learned distribution identifies the symmetry subgroup. This unifies continuous and discrete symmetries under one flow-matching framework, in contrast to prior generator-estimation approaches (e.g., LieGAN's Gaussian prior over algebra coefficients).

The paper identifies and analyzes a genuinely interesting phenomenon ('last-minute mode convergence') for discrete subgroups, supported by a controlled experiment on SO(2)→C4 group elements (Appendix D), and proposes a simple, effective power time schedule that is ablated over skewness (Appendix E.1).

Empirical results are strong where they matter: LieFlow substantially outperforms LieGAN on all discrete groups (e.g., SO(3)→Tet 0.089 vs 2.326; Ico 0.118 vs 1.861) on both synthetic and real ModelNet10 data, while remaining comparable on continuous subgroups. The masking experiments (Table 3) demonstrate useful robustness to incomplete observations.

The paper is generally clear, provides full training/sampling algorithms (Algs. 1-3), the target-field derivation (Appendix A), dataset and architecture details, and an honest limitations/LLM-usage statement.

The framework naturally accommodates partial symmetries via the conditional interpretation of the generated group elements, and the 2D partial-C4 result suggests the method can recover group closure beyond observed elements.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim—that the flow-matching objective 'implicitly filters out transformations that are not true symmetries' because inconsistent targets 'cancel out'—is asserted only heuristically (Sec. 4.1). No proof or formal analysis shows why the learned marginal field's support should coincide with H rather than, e.g., an arbitrary subset of G. This is the load-bearing claim of the paper and it is not rigorously established.

The method assumes the hypothesis group G contains H, and results depend strongly on the choice of G and its prior (the GL(2)+ 'L' vs 'M' sampling gives 1.321 vs 0.428 in Table 1). There is no principled guidance for choosing G or its prior in practice, which limits applicability when the true symmetry is not obviously contained in a known group.

Only a single baseline (LieGAN) is compared, despite several relevant contemporaneous methods being discussed (Ko et al. 2024, Shaw et al. 2024, Allingham et al. 2024, Karjol et al. 2024). The empirical case for 'significantly outperforming state-of-the-art' rests on one comparison.

There is no systematic procedure to extract the actual algebraic structure of the discovered group (generators, closure, order). 'Discovery' is reported qualitatively via histograms/support for discrete groups and Wasserstein distance to ground truth, so it is unclear how the method would report a continuous subgroup or verify group axioms in a new dataset.

Some claims are under-supported: the 'recovery of the full closure C4' from only three observed rotations is surprising and its mechanism is not explained (could be an artifact of the marginal field); and there is no control experiment on a genuinely symmetry-free dataset to confirm the method returns the trivial group rather than an arbitrary support.

Scope is narrow: experiments are limited to small point clouds (128 points) with small hypothesis groups (SO(2), GL(2)+, SO(3)) and a handful of canonical objects. Scalability to higher-dimensional or non-compact groups, and to settings where H is not a known subgroup of a prescribed G, is left untested and acknowledged only briefly.

Presentation issues: Figure 2's subplot labeling/caption is inconsistent (the text references '(d)' as part of a figure whose caption describes (a)-(c)), and Figure 3 packs many subplots with limited legibility; no code release is mentioned to aid reproducibility.

strengths: Novel and conceptually appealing framing of symmetry discovery as distribution learning on a hypothesis Lie group via flow matching, which unifies continuous and discrete symmetry discovery and avoids assuming a fixed Lie algebra basis or a fixed coefficient distribution (unlike LieGAN).

Identifies and analyzes an interesting 'last-minute convergence' phenomenon for discrete subgroups, and proposes a simple, effective power time-scheduling fix (with an ablation on the skewness parameter n).

Consistent and substantial improvements over LieGAN on discrete groups (e.g., Tet 0.089 vs 2.326; Ico 0.118 vs 1.861) across synthetic 2D/3D and ModelNet10, with a reasonably fair baseline setup (matched architectures) and a principled Wasserstein-1 metric for generated group elements.

Honest discussion of limitations (small point clouds, few objects, sensitivity to prior parameterization) and useful auxiliary analyses (masking robustness, posterior entropy, time-progression visualizations).
weaknesses: Scope is very limited: hypothesis groups are restricted to SO(2), GL(2)+, and SO(3), and data to 2D/3D point clouds (128 points). Scalability to higher-dimensional, non-compact, or larger Lie groups—the main practical need—is not demonstrated, yet the abstract/contributions claim broad coverage of 'continuous, discrete, approximate, and partially observed symmetries.'

The load-bearing claim that the flow-matching objective 'implicitly filters out transformations that are not true symmetries' and that the support of the learned distribution recovers H is supported only by intuitive reasoning (inconsistent targets cancel out); there is no formal or empirical verification of this mechanism. If this intuition fails, the method's guarantees collapse.

The 'real-world' ModelNet10 experiment does not actually discover natural symmetries: symmetries are induced by applying known group transformations to canonical shapes, so the ground-truth group is known by construction and evaluation is effectively synthetic. This weakens the claim of real-world applicability.

High sensitivity to the prior over G that is not resolved: GL(2)+→C4 gives W1 = 1.321 with Lie-algebra-coefficient sampling versus 0.428 with matrix-composition sampling, an order-of-magnitude gap driven purely by the prior choice.

Only one baseline (LieGAN), which is not designed for discrete groups (it requires a hand-crafted multi-modal prior); the discrete-group comparison may therefore overstate the advance. No comparison to other recent symmetry-discovery methods (Allingham et al. 2024; Shaw et al. 2024; Ko et al. 2024) that the paper itself cites as closely related.

The 'last-minute convergence' analysis (Appendix D) is performed on a toy scalar SO(2)→C4 problem with flow matching directly on group elements, not in the actual Lie-group-acting-on-data setting used in the method; transferability of the diagnosis and the fix is not established.

The power time schedule with n=5 is chosen empirically and applied to all 3D experiments without a principled criterion; the schedule effectively encodes a task-specific inductive bias about where the learning signal lies.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no mention of code/data release, and key experimental details (number of evaluation samples, seeds, metric implementation specifics, compute for synthetic runs) are sparse. The bijectivity assumption in Appendix A (trivial stabilizer) is not empirically checked for symmetric real-world shapes.

The partially observed symmetry experiment is trivial (removing a single element from C4 and recovering the closure), which does not convincingly support the broader claim of handling 'partially observed' or 'approximate' symmetries.

strengths: Novel and principled formulation of symmetry discovery as distribution learning on Lie groups via flow matching, which unifies continuous, discrete, partial, and approximate symmetry discovery in a single framework without assuming a fixed Lie algebra basis or a specific coefficient distribution.

Strong empirical results: LieFlow substantially outperforms the LieGAN baseline on discrete symmetries (e.g., SO(3)→Ico: 0.118 vs. 1.861 on the synthetic tetrahedron; 0.156 vs. 1.828 on ModelNet10) while remaining competitive on continuous subgroups, and is robust to incomplete observations (only moderate degradation at 10% masking).

Identification and careful analysis of the 'last-minute convergence' phenomenon for discrete groups, supported by a posterior/entropy analysis on SO(2)→C4 and velocity phase portraits, leading to a simple and effective power time schedule with a skewness ablation.

Well-organized presentation with clear algorithms (training, generation, group element generation), informative visualizations (Mollweide projections of SO(3) elements), and thorough appendices providing derivations, dataset details, and additional results.

Good reproducibility: detailed architecture, optimizer, learning-rate, and training-time settings are reported, and the method's assumptions (hypothesis group G, prior choice) are explicitly discussed.

The framework naturally extends to partially observed symmetries by treating the discovered distribution as a conditional p_θ(·|x), and the experiments confirm recovery of the full C4 group closure even when only three transformations are observed.
weaknesses: The central claim that the flow-matching objective causes the learned distribution to concentrate on the true symmetry subgroup H is justified only heuristically via a 'cancellation of inconsistent targets' argument; no formal guarantee, bound, or convergence result is provided.

The evaluation relies on a single baseline (LieGAN). Comparisons to other relevant symmetry-discovery methods (e.g., Ko et al. 2024, Shaw et al. 2024, Benton et al. 2020) are missing, which weakens the claim of state-of-the-art performance.

Limited scale and scope: experiments are restricted to small point clouds (2D arrows, irregular tetrahedra, 128-point ModelNet10). Scalability to high-dimensional data or non-compact groups is not demonstrated, as the authors acknowledge.

The method requires the user to specify a hypothesis group G that contains the true symmetry group H, which is a nontrivial form of prior knowledge; performance is sensitive to this choice and to the parameterization/prior, as evidenced by the large gap between the GL(2) Lie-algebra-coefficient (1.321) and matrix-composition (0.428) samplings.
The power time schedule introduces a hyperparameter (skewness n) that must be tuned, and the analysis motivating it is empirical rather than theoretical.

No downstream evaluation is provided to show that the discovered symmetries actually improve equivariant network performance, sample efficiency, or generalization—the stated motivation for symmetry discovery.

strengths: Novel formulation of symmetry discovery as distribution learning on Lie groups via flow matching, enabling a unified treatment of continuous and discrete symmetries within a single framework.
Identifies and analyzes the 'last-minute convergence' phenomenon for discrete symmetries, and proposes a practical power time schedule that substantially improves discrete group discovery.
Strong empirical results across synthetic 2D/3D point clouds, ModelNet10, and real-world MI-Motion data, with large improvements over LieGAN on discrete symmetries and robustness to noise/masking.
Handles partially observed symmetries through conditional distributions over the hypothesis group, with illustrative 2D experiments.
Clear algorithms, detailed derivations, and extensive appendices covering training details, hyperparameters, and additional visualizations, supporting reproducibility.
Honest limitations discussion and impact statement, including risks of biased or incorrect symmetry discovery.
weaknesses: Theoretical support relies on strong assumptions (ideal flow-matching convergence, globally generated support, point stabilizers contained in H); the central claim that the support of the learned distribution recovers H is not proven under practical optimization or finite samples.
The claim of 'without assuming a fixed Lie algebra basis' is overstated: the method still assumes a known hypothesis group G, a prior p(G), and a parameterization of the Lie algebra.

Baseline comparisons are limited: only LieGAN on synthetic data, and SGM/Augerino only on ModelNet10; no comparison to other recent symmetry discovery methods such as Ko et al. (2024) or Shaw et al. (2024), nor to discrete-symmetry-specific approaches.
Partial symmetry handling is demonstrated only on 2D toy examples, without quantitative metrics or extension to 3D/real-world data.
The power time schedule is a heuristic requiring manual tuning of the skewness parameter n, with no principled selection or adaptive scheme; its effect on continuous groups is not ablated.
The Wasserstein-1 metric against ground-truth group elements may not fully capture support recovery, and the ground-truth distribution for continuous subgroups is not clearly specified.
No code release is mentioned, and the disclosed use of LLMs for parts of the model code and most visualization code raises reproducibility concerns.
Scalability to higher-dimensional, non-compact, or more complex hypothesis groups is not demonstrated and remains an open limitation.

strengths: Conceptually appealing and reasonably novel framing: symmetry discovery as distribution learning on a hypothesis Lie group via flow matching, operating directly in group space without a fixed Lie algebra basis or a prescribed coefficient distribution.
Unified treatment of continuous, discrete, and partially observed symmetries, plus a robustness analysis under point masking and SO(3) perturbations (Table 3).

Strong and clearly visualized empirical results in controlled settings: recovery of C4 (Fig. 2), Tet/Oct/Ico/SO(2) on SO(3) (Fig. 3, Table 5), and the semi-synthetic ModelNet10 experiments (Table 2) where LieFlow clearly beats SGM, Augerino, and LieGAN on discrete groups.

The identification of the 'last-minute mode convergence' phenomenon for discrete subgroups, supported by an analysis on SO(2)->C4 (Figs. 9-14), together with a simple and effective power time-schedule whose skewness is ablated (Table 4, Fig. 17), is a useful practical contribution.
Clear writing, well-organized algorithms, informative figures (Mollweide projections, angle histograms), and an honest limitations/impact discussion.
weaknesses: The theoretical support is essentially tautological. Theorem B.4 derives support(p_theta) subset of H from Assumptions B.1-B.3, but B.1 (generated samples stay in support), B.2 ((Gx) cap S = Hx), and B.3 (point stabilizers are global symmetries) already encode the conclusion, so the proposition adds formalism rather than insight. The core mechanism ('inconsistent targets cancel out so only globally consistent transformations admit a coherent field') is heuristic and unproven.

Identifiability problem is not adequately addressed. Since x_t = g^{1-t} x_1, the regression target A = log(g^{-1}) is not a single-valued function of the network input (x_t, t); it is multi-valued modulo the data's own symmetry/stabilizer structure. The model can only learn a conditional expectation, and the claim that this expectation concentrates on H is asserted rather than derived. This is exactly what the 'last-minute convergence' discussion reveals, but the paper does not turn this into a rigorous statement.

The headline comparison against LieGAN on discrete groups is arguably a modeling-mismatch artifact rather than evidence of genuine superiority: LieGAN assumes a unimodal coefficient distribution and, as the authors themselves note, requires a carefully chosen multi-modal prior to represent discrete groups. Comparing against a baseline known to be structurally incapable of the task inflates the reported advantage. Discrete-capable baselines (e.g., Karjol et al. 2024; Zhou et al. 2020; Shaw et al. 2024) are not quantitatively compared.

The 'real-world' evaluation on MI-Motion has no ground-truth symmetry; the approximate C4 around z is inferred/assumed by the authors, and the only comparison is a histogram against LieGAN's near-uniform output. This does not constitute a rigorous validation of discovery in real data.

The ModelNet10 experiments are only semi-synthetic: data are generated by applying sampled group transformations to canonical shapes, so they test recovery of an imposed symmetry rather than discovery of natural symmetries. The 'real-world objects' framing overstates what is actually demonstrated.

Reproducibility concerns: no code/artifact release is mentioned, and the disclosure that LLMs generated parts of the model code and most of the visualization code raises verifiability questions for the empirical claims.

Presentation/consistency issues: the main-text quantitative results for the synthetic 3D experiments are relegated to Appendix Table 5 while Section 5.4 cites 'Table 5'; the RI metric in Table 1 is potentially misleading because W_random differs by roughly an order of magnitude between the (L) and (M) GL(2) sampling strategies, producing e.g. an 80.5% RI for a single-generator LieGAN.

Practical reach is limited: the method yields a distribution rather than an explicit algebraic presentation of the group, and results depend strongly on the hypothesis group (SO(2) W1=0.054 vs GL(2)(L) W1=0.926 in Table 1), which the authors acknowledge but do not resolve.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated formulation of symmetry discovery as distribution learning on Lie groups via flow matching, enabling unified discovery of continuous, discrete, and partially observed symmetries without assuming a fixed Lie algebra basis or a specific coefficient distribution.
Identifies and addresses the 'last-minute convergence' phenomenon for discrete symmetries with a simple yet effective power time schedule, supported by empirical analysis and ablation studies.

Strong and consistent empirical results across synthetic 2D/3D point clouds, ModelNet10, and the real-world MI-Motion dataset. LieFlow significantly outperforms LieGAN, SGM, and Augerino on discrete symmetry discovery while remaining competitive on continuous symmetries.

Provides a theoretical support recovery result (Theorem B.4) with clearly stated assumptions and an honest discussion of its limitations, including the treatment of point stabilizers and partial symmetries.
Demonstrates robustness to noise via masking and perturbation experiments, showing graceful degradation rather than catastrophic failure.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported: detailed architectures, hyperparameters, training times, dataset construction, and an explicit LLM usage statement are provided in the appendix.
Clear presentation with helpful visualizations (e.g., Mollweide projections for SO(3), time progression of flows) that make the method and results accessible.
weaknesses: The theoretical result only guarantees that the learned support is a subset of the true symmetry group H, not that it equals H. Thus the claim that the support 'reveals' H is stronger than what is proven; completeness of discovery is not theoretically established.

The theory relies on strong assumptions (ideal convergence, globally generated support, point stabilizers are global symmetries) that may not hold in practice, and it does not cover the partial symmetry setting that the method empirically addresses.

The training objective regresses a Lie algebra element rather than the data-space velocity field, with the equivalence relying on injectivity of the infinitesimal action. The choice of Riemannian metric on the Lie algebra and its relationship to the data-space metric is not fully discussed.

Lacks experimental comparison to several recent symmetry discovery methods (e.g., Ko et al. 2024; Shaw et al. 2024) that also target continuous and/or discrete symmetries, which could provide a more comprehensive evaluation.

The method requires a hypothesis group G to be specified in advance, which is a form of prior knowledge and limits applicability when the true symmetry group is not contained in a known larger group. Scaling to high-dimensional or non-compact groups remains challenging.
No code release is mentioned, which may hinder full reproducibility despite the detailed training descriptions.
Evaluation on the real-world MI-Motion dataset is qualitative only, without a quantitative ground-truth metric, though this is understandable given the lack of ground-truth symmetry labels.
